new_statements.rule_in_words: Kisi is a tone language (two level + two contour tones, marginal extra-high) with contrastive vowel length; the prosodic inventory contains no word stress and no statement of stress placement is made. 'Stress' is mentioned only as a phrase-level focus device. Independently, Samarin 1950 (p. 90, saved file) lists the phonemes as 'consonants, vowels, tones, and juncture features' with three register tonemes (p. 96) and never uses the word stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Childs notes Northern Kisi differs phonologically from the described Southern variety (phonemic /r/ in the north; different scope of the l→t dissimilation rule; heavier Mandingo admixture), p. 10.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (lexical on nouns, grammatical on verbs); the one 'stress' remark concerns focus marking at utterance level, not word stress. Both opened primary descriptions (Childs 1995, Samarin 1950) describe Liberian = Southern Kisi [kss, sout2778], not Northern Kissi proper; no opened source gives a first-hand prosodic description of the Northern (Guinea/Sierra Leone) variety.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened primary descriptions (Childs 1995; Samarin 1950) describe the Liberian = Southern Kisi variety, Glottolog sout2778 [kss]; Glottolog attaches Samarin 1950 to both kqs and kss. Northern Kissi (kisiduei; Guinea Kissidougou/Guéckédou and Sierra Leone Kailahun; Ethnologue dialects Liaro, Kama, Teng, Tung) is explicitly a distinct, phonologically different dialect per Childs 1995: 9-10, and no opened source gives a first-hand prosodic description of it. The only kqs-specific file opened (Tamba 2023, Sierra Leone) is silent on stress and tone.

new_statements.quote: The most important feature of Kisi's suprasegmental inventory is the use of tone to signal lexical and grammatical differences. [...] The tonal system of Kisi has two level tones and two contour tones, which are transparently derived from level tones in some cases. Furthermore, the high tone is the "marked" tone, as is the case with the majority of tonal systems. [...] An unusual, but not unknown, feature is the extra-high tone of Kisi. It is used sparingly in the language, functioning in only a few grammatical contexts. Another suprasegmental feature found in Kisi is contrastive vowel length for all (non-diphthongized) vowels. Consonant gemination can be found in a few morphologically restricted environments. (p. 22) || It is generally true that high tones are found on stressed syllables of borrowed English words, as in the first two examples. (p. 92)

new_statements.relation_note: Language not in the catalog; agrees with the existing statement from Childs 1995 (tone language, no stress statement) and is its direct predecessor text (the 1995 §2.1.2 paragraph is nearly verbatim the 1988 §2.1.2). Same-dialect caveat: the dissertation's data are Liberian (Southern) Kisi, Foya area, fieldwork 1983-84 (App. E pp. 373-374), i.e. sout2778 rather than nort2765; App. B (pp. 371-372) lists lexical and phonological Northern/Southern differences but nothing prosodic.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kisi is described as a tone language: two level tones (H, L), two contour tones (rise, fall), a grammatically restricted extra-high tone, contrastive vowel length and limited gemination; intonation contours (downdrift, final fall, rise-fall on long question words) override lexical tone. Word stress is never posited for Kisi; the word 'stress' appears only for English (aspiration before English stressed vowels, p. 45; English stressed syllables surfacing as H tone in loans, p. 92). 'Accent' occurs only for dialect (p. 12) and for an accentual analysis of verb tone (p. 110, Low-toned verb syllables as 'non-accented', citing Childs 1988a on the extra-high tone as 'a new system of prominence?').
new_statements.exceptions: none; ideophones show 'expressive intonation' features (raised/lowered register, exaggerated pitch range, duration, rate; §4.8.2.1 p. 174) but no stress is attributed to them either
new_statements.identity_note: Childs 1988 dissertation: data from Southern/Liberian Kisi (Foya area, Liberia; informants listed in Appendix E, pp. 373-374; one Guinean assistant from Kissidougou 'experienced no problems of intelligibility with the Liberian Kisi', p. 13). Childs distinguishes a Northern (Guinea: Kissidougou/Guekedou) and a Southern (Liberia, Sierra Leone) dialect (pp. 12-13); Appendix B (pp. 371-372) gives lexical (kala/sEwaa vs poonyaa 'write') and phonological (botteng/bolleng 'head', kimbu/cimbu 'steal') differences, no prosodic difference. So the tonal description applies directly to sout2778 and only by extension to nort2765; nothing in the dissertation suggests the northern dialect differs in tone/stress type. The JALL abstract says Kisi is 'spoken primarily in the Republic of Guinea' but the author's data are Liberian.
